planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, where the subtle leaf banding shows best away from harsh midday sun.

directions: Hawk's Feather is an older, rare selection of lilyturf grown not for flashy color contrast but for an unusual transverse mottling pattern — irregular pale yellow to cream bands crossing the dark green blades rather than running lengthwise, evoking the barred wing feathers of a hawk. The effect is subtle and best appreciated up close, since the pattern can look almost like leaf stress from a distance. Clumps are slow to bulk up and stay well-behaved, making this a connoisseur's plant for a shaded collector's bed rather than a mass groundcover. Lavender flower spikes appear in summer but are secondary to the foliage interest. This selection served as the seed parent for the more strongly banded cultivar 'Sideswiped'. Divide congested clumps in spring and remove tattered winter foliage before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; the horizontal gold banding is most vivid on fresh new growth.

directions: Sideswiped stands apart from the many longitudinally striped liriopes by carrying its variegation crosswise — broad, irregular bands of bright yellow slash horizontally over the upright, dark green blades, most pronounced on newly emerging leaves and softening as foliage ages. The plant was selected over roughly two decades from a seedling of the rare 'Hawk's Feather', chosen for its bolder, wider banding, and only released once breeders confirmed the trait held true from division to division. Clumping and well-mannered rather than a runner, it works best as an accent or specimen clump rather than a solid-sheet groundcover, since the bold pattern can look busy in large masses. Short spikes of lavender flowers appear above the foliage in midsummer. Grow it in a sheltered shade bed where the unusual leaf pattern can be viewed up close, and divide in spring once clumps become crowded.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this compact selection tolerates more sun than most lilyturf cultivars.

directions: Purple Explosion is a patented (PP21,352), tightly compact lilyturf bred for an unusually heavy bloom display, with dense, narrow, deep green foliage topped by thick spikes of intensely colored violet-purple flowers that open simultaneously for a dramatic, uniform show rather than the staggered bloom typical of older cultivars. Its tight clumping habit and smaller stature compared with vigorous older selections make it well suited to edging walkways, container plantings, and mass border plantings where a neat, floriferous groundcover is wanted. It shows notably good resistance to powdery mildew and root rot compared with many liriope selections, and once established tolerates moderate drought and deer browsing pressure. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to keep clumps looking fresh for the next bloom cycle.

common_name: Merton Jacobs Giant Lilyturf (Supergreen Giant Lilyturf)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this large-growing selection benefits from generous spacing to show off its bold clumping form.

directions: Merton Jacobs is a patented (PP12,068) selection of giant lilyturf, a larger-growing species distinct from the more common Liriope muscari, discovered as a chance seedling in the mid-1990s and valued for building dense, substantial clumps noticeably faster than the parent species. Tall, leafless stems carry long racemes of violet to blue-violet flowers well above the arching, dark green, grass-like foliage in summer, followed by dark purple berries that persist into fall and attract birds. Lacking above-ground stems of its own, the plant forms a tidy, fountain-like clump rather than spreading aggressively, making it suitable as a bold specimen or accent groundcover rather than a running ground cover. It tolerates full shade but develops its fullest flower display with a few hours of morning sun, and like other liriopes shrugs off heat, humidity, and root competition from nearby trees. Shear back tattered foliage in late winter before new shoots emerge.
